reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / Low's Clinical Autonomic Disorders
clinicalPearls: A fall in systolic blood pressure, conventionally at least 20 mmHg, within about two hours of eating, or a fall below a symptomatic threshold
Symptoms include light-headedness, weakness, visual disturbance, falls, or syncope after meals, and angina in susceptible patients
Particularly common in older people and in those with autonomic failure, Parkinson disease, or diabetes
Large, carbohydrate-rich meals and alcohol are the strongest provokers
An important but often overlooked cause of postprandial falls and syncope in the elderly
Frequently coexists with orthostatic hypotension, which compounds the risk
Diagnosis rests on measuring blood pressure before and serially after a standardised meal
Management is non-pharmacological first: smaller, more frequent, lower-carbohydrate meals, adequate water intake before meals, reduced alcohol, and avoiding standing soon after eating
reference.pathophysiology: After a meal, blood pools in the splanchnic circulation as digestion increases mesenteric blood flow, and vasoactive gastrointestinal peptides promote splanchnic vasodilatation. In a healthy person the baroreflex compensates through increased sympathetic outflow, vasoconstriction elsewhere, and a modest rise in heart rate, keeping blood pressure stable. In postprandial hypotension this compensation is inadequate, typically because of impaired baroreflex or sympathetic function as in autonomic failure, ageing, diabetes, or Parkinson disease, so that splanchnic pooling causes a sustained fall in blood pressure. Rapid gastric emptying and carbohydrate-rich meals, which accelerate the insulin and gut-peptide response, exaggerate the effect.
additionalDifferentials: Cardiac arrhythmia or structural heart disease
additionalInvestigations: Serial blood-pressure measurement before and after a standardised meal
Lying-to-standing blood pressure to detect coexisting orthostatic hypotension
Medication review, particularly of antihypertensives and diuretics taken with meals
Autonomic function testing where autonomic failure is suspected
ECG and ambulatory monitoring to exclude arrhythmia
Blood glucose assessment around symptomatic episodes
redFlags: Postprandial angina or evidence of cardiac ischaemia
Marked coexisting orthostatic hypotension suggesting autonomic failure
Neurological features suggesting an underlying synucleinopathy
reference.prognosis: Postprandial hypotension is usually manageable with dietary and behavioural measures, but in frail older people and those with autonomic failure it is an important, sometimes recurrent cause of falls, syncope, and reduced quality of life.
pitfalls: Overlooking meals as the trigger for falls or syncope in older patients
Timing antihypertensive medication so that its peak effect coincides with the postprandial fall
Failing to look for coexisting orthostatic hypotension
Attributing symptoms solely to hypoglycaemia without measuring blood pressure
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Advise smaller, more frequent meals lower in rapidly absorbed carbohydrate and reduced alcohol intake to lessen splanchnic blood pooling
Recommend behavioural measures such as drinking water before meals, remaining seated after eating and avoiding exertion in the postprandial period
Review and reschedule antihypertensives and diuretics away from mealtimes, or reduce their dose
Consider acarbose to slow carbohydrate absorption, caffeine as an adjunct, and octreotide in refractory autonomic failure
Identify and manage coexisting orthostatic hypotension, which compounds the risk of falls and syncope
Optimise treatment of the underlying condition such as autonomic failure, Parkinson disease or diabetes with the relevant specialist
